Today students read the crossing itself alongside Virgil's classical version to see what Riordan keeps and what he updates.","enduringUnderstanding":"Writers retell old stories to speak to new audiences, keeping familiar elements while changing details, setting and tone to reflect their own world.","futureLessons":"Lesson 27 moves to Chapter 19 (pp. 300–309) and the updated afterlife. Students will use today's habit of comparing a source and an adaptation, and of naming a theme with an abstract noun, in later cross-text writing.","performanceTask":"Shared Stories, Shared Lessons asks for cross-text comparison and adaptation analysis. Turn to a partner and describe in one or two sentences how the underworld felt to Percy when he arrived."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What words would you use to describe the mood of the underworld so far in the novel?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It feels strange and kind of funny, but also creepy. It's like a boring office building, but everybody there is dead, so it's also hopeless."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Riordan did not invent the underworld. Ancient writers described it thousands of years ago. Today we compare his crossing to the Roman poet Virgil's version and write about what Riordan keeps and what he changes."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Do not preview the Aeneid details; students will discover them in the Literacy Lab and Learning in Action."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach abstract nouns as thematic anchors in topic sentences and review pronoun shifts, using mentor sentences tied to the crossing.","activities":[{"id":"lab-abstract-nouns","title":"Abstract Nouns as Thematic Anchors","minutes":6,"standards":["W.6.2.a","W.6.2.d","L.6.6"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read the two topic sentences with your teacher. Decide which one gives a clearer idea of what the paragraph will be about, and underline the abstract noun."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"An abstract noun names an idea you cannot touch, like justice, apathy, betrayal, loyalty, destiny or authority. In analytical writing, an abstract noun anchors your topic sentence. It tells the reader the big idea your evidence will prove."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Sentence A: Both texts have a river and a boatman. Sentence B: Both Virgil and Riordan use the crossing to the underworld to show the authority of death over everyone who arrives."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which sentence is stronger, and which word anchors the idea?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Sentence B is stronger because it says what the crossing means, not just what is in it. The word authority anchors it, since death is in charge in both stories."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which abstract noun from our list could anchor a sentence about the souls waiting to cross, and why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Destiny, because the souls cannot choose. They have to wait for the ferryman to take them. Apathy could also work for the modern version if nobody seems to care."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"This is the designated foundational skills focus and can double as the ELD lesson. Accept any abstract noun a student can defend with the text."}]},{"id":"lab-pronoun-shifts","title":"Fixing Pronoun Shifts","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.1","L.6.1.c"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A pronoun shift happens when a writer changes person or number in the middle of an idea. For example: When a reader enters the underworld in either text, you feel dread. The sentence starts with a reader, which is third person, and shifts to you, which is second person. Formal writing stays consistent."},{"type":"directions","text":"Fix each sentence so the pronouns stay consistent. 1) When a soul reaches the river, you must wait for the ferryman. 2) Each soul in the Aeneid waits on the bank, and they hope to cross."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How did you correct each sentence?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"For 1, I wrote: When a soul reaches the river, it must wait for the ferryman. For 2, I wrote: Each soul waits on the bank and hopes to cross. Or I could write: All the souls wait on the bank, and they hope to cross."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Remind students to watch for this shift when they draft. In formal comparison writing, they should avoid you and keep to third person."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students gather and analyze evidence from Chapter 18 and the Aeneid excerpt (W.6.2, W.6.9). Part B: Students draft a comparison paragraph with a clear thematic topic sentence and formal style (W.6.2, W.6.4).","activities":[{"id":"lia-evidence-chart","title":"Part A: Gather and Compare Evidence","minutes":15,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.9","RL.6.1","RL.6.4","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 18","pages":"pp. 291–299"},{"type":"text-reference","title":"Translated excerpt from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 6","pages":"lines 295–336"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the crossing scene in Chapter 18 and then the Aeneid excerpt. With a partner, complete a three-column chart with the headings: Detail, Aeneid, The Lightning Thief. Make rows for the crowd of souls, the river or water, and the ferryman. Quote exact words where you can and underline any word that creates a feeling."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does each text show the souls waiting to enter the underworld?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the Aeneid, huge crowds of souls crowd the bank and reach out, wanting to cross. In the novel, the dead are lined up in the DOA building, like people waiting in line. Both show lots of souls who have to wait."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Compare the water and the ferryman. How do the word choices create tone and mood?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Virgil uses words like fathomless for the water and squalid for the ferryman, so the mood is dark, ancient and frightening. Riordan changes the setting to a modern DOA place with a boatman, so the tone is more humorous and ordinary, but the dead still cannot escape."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Riordan honor, and what does he change?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He honors the river, the ferryman and the crowd of souls who must cross. He changes the look and feel by making it modern, so it feels like an office or a business instead of a terrifying ancient place."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Circulate to make sure students pair a quote with each claim. If the excerpt translation differs in wording, have students use the exact words from their copy."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in comparing two texts and evaluating how word choice creates tone and mood (ELD.PI.6.7, ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Model: In the Aeneid, the water is described as fathomless, which makes it feel ___. In the novel, the setting is modern, so the tone feels ___. Have students expand sentences with adverbials: The souls wait anxiously on the bank. The boatman moves slowly across the dark river. Frames: Virgil uses the word ___ to show ___. Riordan changes ___ to ___. Both texts keep ___.","watchFor":"If students only name details without tone, then ask: What feeling does that word give you? If students confuse tone and mood, then say: Tone is the writer's attitude; mood is how the reader feels. Success: students quote a word from each text and explain its feeling."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding comparisons in the Aeneid","tryThis":"Read the excerpt aloud together in short chunks. Give a pre-labeled row (souls, river, ferryman) and have students highlight one phrase per row before discussing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find one detail Riordan changes that Virgil never mentions and explain what it suggests about the modern world."}]},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.9"],"stem":"Which statement best compares how the two texts present the crossing into the underworld?","choices":[{"text":"Both texts keep the ferryman and the dark water, but Riordan sets the crossing in a modern DOA building so the tone feels more ordinary and humorous.","correct":true,"rationale":"This names what is honored (ferryman, water) and what is changed (modern setting, tone)."},{"text":"Virgil's crossing is humorous, while Riordan's is terrifying and ancient.","correct":false,"rationale":"This reverses the tones; Virgil's words like fathomless and squalid create darkness, while Riordan's modern setting adds humor."},{"text":"Riordan leaves out the souls of the dead entirely and focuses only on Percy.","correct":false,"rationale":"The dead are still present in the novel's crossing scene; the chapter shows many souls waiting."},{"text":"Both texts are exactly the same, with only the names changed.","correct":false,"rationale":"The texts share elements, but Riordan changes the setting and tone, so they are not identical."}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-paragraph","title":"Part B: Draft the Comparison Paragraph","minutes":15,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.4","W.6.2.a","W.6.2.b","W.6.2.c","W.6.2.d","W.6.2.e","W.6.2.f","W.6.5","W.6.10"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Watch how I plan. My topic sentence names both texts and an abstract noun: Riordan honors Virgil's picture of death's authority over every soul but changes the setting to fit a modern world. Next I add evidence from each text, then transitions like similarly, however and as a result. I end with a concluding sentence about what the change shows."},{"type":"directions","text":"Using your chart, write one explanatory paragraph (6 to 8 sentences) that compares Riordan's modern underworld crossing with Virgil's classical version and explains how the novel both honors and changes the older myth. Include: a topic sentence with an abstract noun; at least one quotation or detail from each text; at least two transitions; precise words about tone and mood; consistent pronouns and a formal style; and a concluding sentence."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Riordan honors the classical idea of death's authority over every soul but changes the setting to fit a modern world. In Virgil's Aeneid, crowds of souls gather by a fathomless river, and a squalid ferryman decides who may cross, which creates a dark and fearful mood. Similarly, in The Lightning Thief, the dead must wait and a boatman carries them across the water. However, Riordan places the crossing in a modern DOA building, so the tone feels more ordinary and even humorous. Even so, the dead still have no power to escape. As a result, Riordan keeps the heart of the old myth while making it feel familiar to a reader today. This shows that old stories can be retold without losing their meaning."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Confer first with students who list details without comparing. Ask: What does Riordan keep? What does he change? Then check pronouns for you-shifts."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a formal comparison paragraph with expanded sentences and precise language (ELD.PI.6.10, ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Have students rehearse the topic sentence aloud first. Frames: Riordan honors ___ but changes ___. In the Aeneid, ___ creates a ___ mood. Similarly, ___. However, ___. As a result, ___. Expand with adverbials: In the novel, the dead wait quietly in line. In Virgil's version, the souls crowd desperately along the bank.","watchFor":"If students copy from the text, then say: Close the book and tell me the idea in your words. If students use only then and and, then offer similarly, however, as a result. Success: the paragraph names what is kept and changed, with evidence from both texts."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: starting the paragraph","tryThis":"Provide the starter: Riordan honors the myth of ___ by keeping ___, but he changes ___ to show ___. Let students rehearse one sentence at a time orally before writing."},{"type":"Ready for extension"==="x"?{}:{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a sentence explaining how a second abstract noun, such as apathy or destiny, also connects the two crossings, and to use a precise verb like reimagines or transforms."}]},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Checklist: topic sentence with an abstract noun; evidence from both texts; transitions that show comparison and contrast; precise words about tone and mood; formal style with consistent pronouns; concluding sentence."}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how comparing two versions of a setting reveals tone and prepares them for the performance task.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-turn-and-talk","title":"What Changes and What Stays?","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.2","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Share your topic sentence with a partner. Tell your partner which abstract noun you chose and why it fits both texts."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why is it useful to compare an old version of a story with a modern one?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Comparing shows what the author thinks is important enough to keep and what needs to change for new readers. It also helps you see how word choice changes the mood."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In your Shared Stories, Shared Lessons task, you will compare texts and explain how a story changes across time.
